source.title: Decoding Vision Transformers: The Diffusion Steering Lens
source.authors: Ryota Takatsuki; Sonia Joseph; Ippei Fujisawa; Ryota Kanai

page_placements.theme: Self-repair invoked to explain small ablation effects in CLIP vision transformers

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the Hydra effect as a possible explanation for variability in head-ablation effects, but it does not measure downstream compensation or compare total ablation effects with direct component effects.
record.gate_note: The paper performs attention-head ablations and reports output changes, but those measurements do not establish whether later components change their outputs to restore a prediction. Its DSL and overlay-removal results concern a vision model and are not tests of the listed self-repair versions.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a visualization method (Diffusion Steering Lens) for a CLIP ViT and validates it with head ablations. It measures output change after ablation but never measures downstream compensation, direct versus total effects, or later components restoring outputs. It invokes the Hydra effect only as a speculative explanation for variable ablation effects (Sec 5.2.1). Its evaluation rows assess the authors' own method against baselines, so it does not test any version. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses': the paper mentions the Hydra effect in a single clause.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that DSL visualizes direct submodule contributions in ViTs more reliably than Diffusion Lens. They also conclude that DSL-guided head ablations remove overlay influence, approach an ACDC-like optimum and beat random selection.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns a vision transformer and evaluates a visualization method; it does not implement or reproduce the self-repair measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that DSL outputs are noisy at low steering coefficients and stable for coefficients greater than 10; experiments use 100. It also reports variation in output effects across heads.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ViT-bigG/14, ablating heads whose DSL visualization resembles the input tends to reduce output similarity more. Some high-similarity heads show little effect, which the authors speculatively attribute to the Hydra effect (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a ViT, attention heads whose direct-effect visualization resembles the input have larger ablation effects, with exceptions that may reflect downstream compensation (untested).

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
record.problems: Results relevant to head ablation are reported mainly in figures without numerical values. The experiments use one ViT model and 8 ImageNet Validation samples; the paper does not test downstream self-repair.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported strategy-by-overlay trajectories were added for the supplementary overlays: the text says their results are similar to the flower-overlay result, and only the DSL trajectory rows are retained for those overlays.

untested.parts: All parts: layer ablation with compensation by later attention layers.
All parts: head-level compensation on general text. The study uses a vision model only.
All parts: degree, prompt variability and overcorrection of compensation are not measured.
All parts: no mechanisms for self-repair are identified.
All parts: ablation type is not compared for compensation.
All parts. The authors only speculate that the Hydra effect explains why some high-similarity heads show small ablation effects; no test is made.

record.verdict_notes: The only link to the phenomenon is one sentence calling variability in ablation effects 'likely' due to the Hydra effect, with citation [30]. Rushing & Nanda is cited only in the introduction, as support for iterative refinement. All results concern one vision model and 8 ImageNet samples, reported in figures only.

versions.untested_parts: Layer-level ablation followed by compensation from later attention layers.
Late-MLP counterbalancing and its response to earlier-component ablation.
Full-distribution head-level self-repair on general text across model families and sizes.
Whether compensation is partial on average, varies by prompt, or sometimes overcorrects.
Whether compensation occurs under on-distribution ablations.
Whether self-repair makes ablation-based importance scores misstate a component's role.
